{{Short description|Formula in Lie theory}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula''' gives a value of <math>Z</math> that solves the equation
<math display="block">e^X e^Y = e^Z</math>
for possibly [[noncommutative]] {{mvar|''X''}} and {{mvar|''Y''}} in the [[Lie algebra]] of a [[Lie group]]. There are various ways of writing the formula, but all ultimately yield an expression for <math>Z</math> in Lie algebraic terms, that is, as a formal series (not necessarily convergent) in <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> and iterated commutators thereof. The first few terms of this series are:
<math display="block">Z = X + Y + \frac{1}{2} [X,Y] + \frac{1}{12} [X,[X,Y]] + \frac{1}{12} [Y,[Y,X]] + \cdots\,,</math>
where "<math>\cdots</math>" indicates terms involving higher [[Commutator#Identities_(ring_theory)|commutators]] of <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>. If <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are sufficiently small elements of the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g</math> of a Lie group <math>G</math>, the series is convergent. Meanwhile, every element <math>g</math> sufficiently close to the identity in <math>G</math> can be expressed as <math>g = e^X</math> for a small <math>X</math> in <math>\mathfrak g</math>. Thus, we can say that ''near the identity'' the group multiplication in <math>G</math>—written as <math>e^X e^Y = e^Z</math>—can be expressed in purely Lie algebraic terms. The Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula can be used to give comparatively simple proofs of deep results in the [[Lie group–Lie algebra correspondence]].

If <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are sufficiently small <math>n \times n</math> matrices, then <math>Z</math> can be computed as the logarithm of <math>e^X e^Y</math>, where the exponentials and the logarithm can be computed as [[power series]]. The point of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula is then the highly nonobvious claim that <math>Z := \log \left(e^X e^Y\right)</math> can be expressed as a series in repeated commutators of <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>.

Modern expositions of the formula can be found in, among other places, the books of Rossmann<ref>{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002}}</ref> and Hall.<ref name="Hall 2015">{{harvnb|Hall|2015}}</ref>

== History ==
The formula is named after [[Henry Frederick Baker]], [[John Edward Campbell]], and [[Felix Hausdorff]] who stated its qualitative form, i.e. that only commutators and commutators of commutators, ad infinitum, are needed to express the solution. An earlier statement of the form was adumbrated  by [[Friedrich Schur]] in 1890<ref>F. Schur (1890), "Neue Begründung der Theorie der endlichen Transformationsgruppen," ''[[Mathematische Annalen]]'', '''35''' (1890), 161–197. [http://www.digizeitschriften.de/dms/img/?PID=GDZPPN002252120 online copy]</ref> where a convergent power series is given, with terms recursively defined.<ref>see, e.g., [[Shlomo Sternberg]], ''[http://www.math.harvard.edu/~shlomo/docs/lie_algebras.pdf Lie Algebras]'' (2004) Harvard University. (''cf p 10.'')</ref> This qualitative form is what is used in the most important applications, such as the relatively accessible proofs of the [[Lie correspondence]] and in [[quantum field theory]]. Following Schur, it was noted in print by Campbell<ref>[[John Edward Campbell]], [[London Mathematical Society#Publications|Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]] '''28''' (1897) 381–390; (cf pp386-7 for the eponymous lemma); J. Campbell, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society 29 (1898) 14–32.</ref> (1897); elaborated by [[Henri Poincaré]]<ref>[[Henri Poincaré]], [[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences]] 128 (1899) 1065–1069; Transactions of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 18 (1899) 220–255. [http://henripoincarepapers.univ-lorraine.fr/chp/hp-pdf/hp1899cp.pdf online]</ref> (1899) and Baker (1902);<ref>[[Henry Frederick Baker]], Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (1) 34 (1902) 347–360; H. Baker, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (1) 35 (1903) 333–374; H. Baker, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (Ser 2) 3 (1905) 24–47.</ref> and systematized geometrically, and linked to the [[Jacobi identity]] by Hausdorff (1906).<ref>[[Felix Hausdorff]], "Die symbolische Exponentialformel in der Gruppentheorie", Ber Verh Saechs Akad Wiss Leipzig 58 (1906) 19–48.</ref> The first actual explicit formula, with all numerical coefficients, is due to [[Eugene Dynkin]] (1947).<ref>{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002}} p. 23</ref> The history of the formula is described in detail in the article of Achilles and Bonfiglioli<ref>{{harvnb|Achilles|Bonfiglioli|2012}}</ref> and in the book of Bonfiglioli and Fulci.<ref>{{harvnb|Bonfiglioli|Fulci|2012}}</ref>

== Explicit forms ==
For many purposes, it is only necessary to know that an expansion for <math>Z</math> in terms of iterated commutators of <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> exists; the exact coefficients are often irrelevant. (See, for example, the discussion of the relationship between [[Lie group–Lie algebra correspondence#The correspondence|Lie group and Lie algebra homomorphisms]] in Section 5.2 of Hall's book,<ref name="Hall 2015"/> where the precise coefficients play no role in the argument.) A remarkably direct existence proof was given by [[Martin Eichler]],<ref name="Eichler_1968">{{cite journal| first=Martin|last=Eichler| author-link=Martin Eichler| year=1968|title=A new proof of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula| journal= Journal of the Mathematical Society of Japan| volume=20|issue=1–2 |pages= 23–25| url=http://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.jmsj/1260463291| doi=10.2969/jmsj/02010023| doi-access=free| url-access=subscription}}</ref> see also the "Existence results" section below.

In other cases, one may need detailed information about <math>Z</math> and it is therefore desirable to compute <math>Z</math> as explicitly as possible. Numerous formulas exist; we will describe two of the main ones (Dynkin's formula and the integral formula of Poincaré) in this section.

===Dynkin formula===
Let ''G'' be a Lie group with Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g</math>. Let
<math display="block">\exp : \mathfrak g \to G </math>
be the [[exponential map (Lie theory)|exponential map]].
The following general combinatorial formula was introduced by [[Eugene Dynkin]] (1947),<ref name="Jacobson" /><ref name="dynkin">{{cite journal| last=Dynkin |first=Eugene Borisovich |author-link=Eugene Dynkin |year=1947 |language=ru |title=Вычисление коэффициентов в формуле Campbell–Hausdorff |trans-title=Calculation of the coefficients in the Campbell–Hausdorff formula | journal=[[Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR]] |volume=57 |pages=323–326}}</ref>
<math display="block">\log(\exp X\exp Y) =
\sum_{n = 1}^\infty\frac {(-1)^{n-1}}{n}
\sum_{\begin{smallmatrix} r_1 + s_1 > 0 \\ \vdots \\ r_n + s_n > 0 \end{smallmatrix}}
\frac{[ X^{r_1} Y^{s_1} X^{r_2} Y^{s_2} \dotsm X^{r_n} Y^{s_n} ]}{\left(\sum_{j = 1}^n (r_j + s_j)\right) \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^n r_i! s_i!},
</math>
where the sum is performed over all nonnegative values of <math>s_i</math> and <math>r_i</math>, and the following notation has been used:
<math display="block"> [ X^{r_1} Y^{s_1} \dotsm X^{r_n} Y^{s_n} ] = [ \underbrace{X,[X,\dotsm[X}_{r_1} ,[ \underbrace{Y,[Y,\dotsm[Y}_{s_1} ,\,\dotsm\, [ \underbrace{X,[X,\dotsm[X}_{r_n} ,[ \underbrace{Y,[Y,\dotsm Y}_{s_n} ]]\dotsm]]</math>
with the understanding that {{math|1=[''X''] := ''X''}}.

The series is not convergent in general; it is convergent (and the stated formula is valid) for all sufficiently small <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>.
Since {{math|1=[''A'', ''A''] = 0}}, the term is zero if <math>s_n > 1</math> or if <math>s_n = 0</math> and <math>r_n > 1</math>.<ref>A.A. Sagle & R.E. Walde, "Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras", Academic Press, New York, 1973. {{ISBN|0-12-614550-4}}.</ref>

The first few terms are well-known, with all higher-order terms involving {{math|[''X'',''Y'']}} and [[commutator]] nestings thereof (thus in the [[Lie algebra]]):

{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation = <math>\begin{align}
Z(X,Y)& = \log(\exp X\exp Y) \\
&{}= X + Y + \frac{1}{2}[X,Y] +
\frac{1}{12}\left ([X,[X,Y]] +[Y,[Y,X]]\right ) \\
&{}\quad
- \frac {1}{24}[Y,[X,[X,Y]]] \\
&{}\quad
- \frac{1}{720}\left([Y,[Y,[Y,[Y,X]]]] + [X,[X,[X,[X,Y]]]] \right)
\\
&{}\quad +\frac{1}{360}\left([X,[Y,[Y,[Y,X]]]] + [Y,[X,[X,[X,Y]]]]\right)\\
&{}\quad
+ \frac{1}{120}\left([Y,[X,[Y,[X,Y]]]] + [X,[Y,[X,[Y,X]]]]\right)\\
&{}\quad
+ \frac{1}{240}\left([X,[Y,[X,[Y,[X, Y]]]]] \right)\\
&{}\quad
+ \frac{1}{720}\left([X,[Y,[X,[X,[X, Y]]]]] - [X,[X,[Y,[Y,[X, Y]]]]] \right)\\
&{}\quad
+ \frac{1}{1440}\left([X,[Y,[Y,[Y,[X, Y]]]]] - [X,[X,[Y,[X,[X, Y]]]]] \right) + \cdots
\end{align}</math>
|cellpadding= 6
|border
|border colour = #0073CF
|background colour=#F9FFF7}}

The above lists all summands of order 6 or lower (i.e. those containing 6 or fewer {{math|''X''}}'s and {{math|''Y''}}'s). The {{math|''X'' ↔ ''Y''}} (anti-)/symmetry in alternating orders of the expansion, follows from {{math|1=''Z''(''Y'', ''X'') = −''Z''(−''X'', −''Y'')}}. A complete elementary proof of this formula can be found in the article on the [[derivative of the exponential map]].

===An integral formula===
There are numerous other expressions for <math>Z</math>, many of which are used in the physics literature.<ref name='magnus' /><ref>{{cite journal|author=Suzuki, Masuo| year=1985|title=Decomposition formulas of exponential operators and Lie exponentials with some applications to quantum mechanics and statistical physics|journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics| volume=26| issue=4| pages=601–612 | doi=10.1063/1.526596| bibcode = 1985JMP....26..601S }}; [[Martinus Veltman|Veltman, M]], [[Gerard 't Hooft|'t Hooft, G]] & [[Bernard de Wit|de Wit, B]] (2007), Appendix D.</ref> A popular integral formula is<ref name="miller">W. Miller, ''Symmetry Groups and their Applications'', [[Academic Press]], New York, 1972, pp 159–161. {{ISBN|0-12-497460-0}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Theorem 5.3</ref>
<math display="block">\log\left(e^X e^Y\right) = X + \left ( \int_0^1 \psi \left ( e^{\operatorname{ad} _X} ~ e^{t \operatorname{ad} _ Y}\right ) dt \right) Y, </math>
involving the [[Bernoulli number#Generating function|generating function for the Bernoulli numbers]],
<math display="block"> \psi(x) ~\stackrel{\text{def}}{=} ~ \frac{x \log x}{x-1}= 1- \sum^\infty_{n=1}
{(1-x)^n \over n (n+1)} ~, </math>
utilized by Poincaré and Hausdorff.<ref group="nb">Recall
<math display="block">\psi(e^y)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty B_n ~ y^n/n! ,</math>
for the [[Bernoulli numbers]], ''B''<sub>0</sub> = 1, ''B''<sub>1</sub> = 1/2, ''B''<sub>2</sub> = 1/6,
''B''<sub>4</sub> = −1/30, ...</ref>

=== Matrix Lie group illustration ===
For a matrix Lie group <math>G \sub \mbox{GL}(n,\mathbb{R})</math> the Lie algebra is the [[tangent space]] of the identity ''I'', and the commutator is simply {{math|1=[''X'', ''Y''] = ''XY'' − ''YX''}}; the exponential map is the [[matrix exponential|standard exponential map of matrices]],
<math display="block">\exp X = e^X = \sum_{n=0}^\infty {\frac{X^n}{n!}}.</math>

When one solves for ''Z'' in
<math display="block">e^Z = e^X e^Y,</math>
using the series expansions for {{math|exp}} and {{math|log}} one obtains a simpler formula:
<math display="block"> Z =
\sum_{n>0}
\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n}
\sum_{\stackrel{r_i+s_i > 0}{1 \le i \le n}}
\frac{X^{r_1}Y^{s_1} \cdots X^{r_n}Y^{s_n}}{r_1!s_1!\cdots r_n!s_n!},
\quad \|X\| + \|Y\| < \log 2, \|Z\| < \log 2.</math><ref group="nb">{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002}} Equation (2) Section 1.3. For matrix Lie algebras over the fields {{math|'''R'''}} and {{math|'''C'''}}, the convergence criterion is that the log series converges for ''both sides'' of {{math|1=''e''<sup>''Z''</sup> = ''e''<sup>''X''</sup>''e''<sup>''Y''</sup>}}. This is guaranteed whenever {{math|{{norm|''X''}} + {{norm|''Y''}} < log 2, {{norm|''Z''}} < log 2}} in the [[Hilbert–Schmidt norm]]. Convergence may occur on a larger domain. See {{harvnb|Rossmann|2002}} p. 24.</ref>
The first, second, third, and fourth order terms are:
* <math display="block">z_1 = X + Y</math>
* <math display="block">z_2 = \frac{1}{2} (XY - YX)</math>
* <math display="block">z_3 = \frac{1}{12} \left(X^2Y + XY^2 - 2XYX + Y^2X + YX^2 - 2YXY\right)</math>
* <math display="block">z_4 = \frac{1}{24} \left(X^2Y^2 - 2XYXY - Y^2X^2 + 2YXYX \right).</math>

The formulas for the various <math>z_j</math>'s is ''not'' the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula. Rather, the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula is one of various expressions for <math>z_j</math>'s ''in terms of repeated commutators of <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>''. The point is that it is far from obvious that it is possible to express each <math>z_j</math> in terms of commutators. (The reader is invited, for example, to verify by direct computation that <math>z_3</math> is expressible as a [[linear combination]] of the two nontrivial third-order commutators of <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>, namely <math>[X,[X,Y]]</math> and <math>[Y,[X,Y]]</math>.) The general result that each <math>z_j</math> is expressible as a combination of commutators was shown in an elegant, recursive way by Eichler.<ref name="Eichler_1968" />

A consequence of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula is the following result about the [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]]:
<math display="block">\operatorname{tr} \log \left(e^X e^Y \right) = \operatorname{tr} X + \operatorname{tr}  Y.  </math>
That is to say, since each <math>z_j</math> with <math>j\geq 2</math> is expressible as a linear combination of commutators, the trace of each such term is zero.

=== Questions of convergence ===
Suppose <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are the following matrices in the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2;\mathbb C)</math> (the space of <math>2\times 2</math> matrices with trace zero):
<math display="block">X=\begin{pmatrix}0&i\pi\\ i\pi&0\end{pmatrix};\quad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}.</math>
Then
<math display="block">e^X e^Y = \begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix}.</math>
It is then not hard to show<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Example 3.41</ref> that there does not exist a matrix <math>Z</math> in <math>\operatorname{sl}(2;\mathbb C)</math> with <math>e^X e^Y = e^Z</math>. (Similar examples may be found in the article of Wei.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wei|first=James |date=October 1963 |title=Note on the Global Validity of the Baker-Hausdorff and Magnus Theorems. |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics  |volume=4 |issue= 10 | pages=1337–1341| bibcode = 1963JMP.....4.1337W |doi = 10.1063/1.1703910 }}</ref>)

This simple example illustrates that the various versions of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula, which give expressions for {{math|''Z''}} in terms of iterated Lie-brackets of {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}}, describe ''formal'' power series whose convergence is not guaranteed. Thus, if one wants {{math|''Z''}} to be an actual element of the Lie algebra containing {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}} (as opposed to a formal power series), one has to assume that {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}} are small. Thus, the conclusion that the product operation on a Lie group is determined by the Lie algebra is only a local statement. Indeed, the result cannot be global, because globally one can have nonisomorphic Lie groups with isomorphic Lie algebras.

Concretely, if working with a matrix Lie algebra and <math>\|\cdot\|</math> is a given [[matrix norm|submultiplicative matrix norm]], convergence is guaranteed<ref name="dynkin" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Biagi|first1=Stefano| last2=Bonfiglioli|first2=Andrea| last3=Matone|first3=Marco| date=2018| title=On the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff Theorem: non-convergence and prolongation issues| journal=Linear and Multilinear Algebra|volume=68 |issue=7 | language=en| pages=1310–1328| doi=10.1080/03081087.2018.1540534| issn=0308-1087| arxiv=1805.10089|s2cid=53585331 }}</ref> if
<math display="block">\|X\| + \|Y\| < \frac{\ln 2} 2.</math>

== Special cases ==
If <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> commute, that is <math>[X, Y]=0</math>, the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula reduces to <math>e^X e^Y = e^{X+Y}</math>.

Another case assumes that <math>[X,Y]</math> commutes with both <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>, as for the [[Nilpotent group|nilpotent]] [[Heisenberg group]]. Then the formula reduces to its ''first three terms''.

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|note=<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Theorem 5.1</ref>|math_statement= 
If <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> commute with their commutator, <math>[X,[X,Y]] = [Y,[X,Y]] = 0</math>, then <math>e^X e^Y = e^{X+Y+\frac{1}{2}[X,Y]}</math>.
}}

This is the degenerate case used routinely in [[quantum mechanics]], as illustrated below and is sometimes known as the '''disentangling theorem'''.<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Gerry | first1 = Christopher | last2 = Knight | first2 = Peter |author-link2 = Peter Knight (physicist) |date=2005 |title=Introductory Quantum Optics |url= |location= |publisher=Cambridge University Press |page=49 |isbn=978-0-521-52735-4 |edition = 1st}}</ref> In this case, there are no smallness restrictions on <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>. This result is behind the "exponentiated commutation relations" that enter into the [[Stone–von Neumann theorem]]. A simple proof of this identity is given below.

Another useful form of the general formula emphasizes expansion in terms of ''Y'' and uses the [[adjoint endomorphism|adjoint]] mapping notation <math>\operatorname{ad}_X(Y)=[X,Y]</math>:
<math display="block">\log(\exp X\exp Y) = X + \frac{\operatorname{ad}_X}{1-e^{-\operatorname{ad}_X}} ~ Y + O\left(Y^2\right)
= X + \operatorname{ad}_{X/2} (1 + \coth \operatorname{ad}_{X/2}) ~ Y + O\left(Y^2\right) ,</math>
which is evident from the integral formula above. (The coefficients of the nested commutators with a single <math>Y</math> are normalized Bernoulli numbers.)

Now assume that the commutator is a multiple of <math>Y</math>, so that <math>[X,Y] = sY</math>. Then all iterated commutators will be multiples of <math>Y</math>, and no quadratic or higher terms in <math>Y</math> appear. Thus, the <math>O\left(Y^2\right)</math> term above vanishes and we obtain:

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|note=<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Exercise 5.5</ref>|math_statement=
If <math>[X,Y] = sY</math>, where <math>s</math> is a complex number with <math>s \neq 2\pi in</math> for all integers <math>n</math>, then we have <math display="block">e^X e^Y = \exp\left( X+\frac{s}{1-e^{-s}}Y\right).</math>
}}

Again, in this case there are no smallness restriction on <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>. The restriction on <math>s</math> guarantees that the expression on the right side makes sense. (When <math>s = 0</math> we may interpret <math display="inline">\lim_{s\to 0} s/(1-e^{-s}) = 1</math>.) We also obtain a simple "braiding identity":
<math display="block">e^{X} e^{Y} = e^{\exp (s) Y} e^{X} ,</math>
which may be written as an adjoint dilation:
<math display="block">e^{X} e^{Y} e^{-X} = e^{\exp (s) \, Y} .</math>

== Existence results ==

If <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are matrices, one can compute <math>Z := \log \left(e^X e^Y\right)</math> using the power series for the exponential and logarithm, with convergence of the series if <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are sufficiently small. It is natural to collect together all terms where the total degree in <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> equals a fixed number <math>k</math>, giving an expression <math>z_k</math>. (See the section "Matrix Lie group illustration" above for formulas for the first several <math>z_k</math>'s.) A remarkably direct and concise, recursive proof that each <math>z_k</math> is expressible in terms of repeated commutators of <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> was given by [[Martin Eichler]].<ref name="Eichler_1968" />

Alternatively, we can give an existence argument as follows. The Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula implies that if {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}} are in some [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak g,</math> defined over any field of [[characteristic 0]] like <math>\Reals</math> or <math>\Complex</math>, then
<math display="block">Z = \log(\exp(X) \exp(Y)),</math>
can formally be written as an infinite sum of elements of <math>\mathfrak g</math>. [This infinite series may or may not converge, so it need not define an actual element {{math|''Z''}} in <math>\mathfrak g</math>.] For many applications, the mere assurance of the existence of this formal expression is sufficient, and an explicit expression for this infinite sum is not needed. This is for instance the case in the [[Representation theory of the Lorentz group#Local existence and uniqueness|Lorentzian]]<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Section 5.7</ref> construction of a Lie [[group representation]] from a [[Lie algebra representation]]. Existence can be seen as follows.

We consider the ring <math>S = \R[[X,Y]]</math> of all [[non-commuting formal power series]] with real coefficients in the non-commuting variables {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}}. There is a [[ring homomorphism]] from {{math|''S''}} to the [[tensor product]] of {{math|''S''}} with {{math|''S''}} over {{math|''R''}},
<math display="block">\Delta \colon S \to S \otimes S,</math>
called the [[coalgebra|coproduct]], such that
<math display="block">\Delta(X) = X \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes X</math> and <math display="block">\Delta(Y) = Y \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes Y.</math>
(The definition of Δ is extended to the other elements of ''S'' by requiring ''R''-linearity, multiplicativity and infinite additivity.)

One can then verify the following properties:
* The map {{math|exp}}, defined by its standard [[Taylor series]], is a bijection between the set of elements of {{math|''S''}} with [[constant term]] 0 and the set of elements of {{math|''S''}} with constant term 1; the inverse of exp is log
* <math>r = \exp(s)</math> is ''grouplike'' (this means <math>\Delta(r) = r\otimes r</math>) [[if and only if]] ''s'' is ''primitive'' (this means <math>\Delta(s) = s\otimes 1 + 1\otimes s</math>).
* The grouplike elements form a [[group (mathematics)|group]] under multiplication.
* The [[primitive element (co-algebra)|primitive elements]] are ''exactly the formal infinite sums of elements of the Lie algebra'' generated by ''X'' and ''Y'', where the Lie bracket is given by the [[commutator]] <math>[U,V] = UV - VU</math>. ([[Kurt Otto Friedrichs|Friedrichs]]' theorem<ref name="magnus">{{Cite journal
| last1 = Magnus | first1 = Wilhelm | title = On the exponential solution of differential equations for a linear operator
| doi = 10.1002/cpa.3160070404 | author-link= Wilhelm Magnus
| journal = [[Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics]]
| volume = 7 | issue = 4 | pages = 649–673| year = 1954}}</ref><ref name="Jacobson">[[Nathan Jacobson]], ''Lie Algebras'', John Wiley & Sons, 1966.</ref>)

The existence of the Campbell–Baker–Hausdorff formula can now be seen as follows:<ref name="Jacobson" />
The elements ''X'' and ''Y'' are primitive, so <math>\exp(X)</math> and <math>\exp(Y)</math> are grouplike; so their product <math>\exp(X)\exp(Y)</math> is also grouplike; so its logarithm <math>\log(\exp(X)\exp(Y))</math> is primitive; and hence can be written as an infinite sum of elements of the Lie algebra generated by {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}}.

The [[universal enveloping algebra]] of the [[free Lie algebra]] generated by {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}} is isomorphic to the algebra of all [[non-commuting polynomial]]s in {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}}. In common with all universal enveloping algebras, it has a natural structure of a [[Hopf algebra]], with a coproduct {{math|Δ}}. The ring {{math|''S''}} used above is just a completion of this Hopf algebra.

== Zassenhaus formula ==
A related combinatoric expansion that is useful in dual<ref name="magnus" /> applications is
<math display="block">e^{t(X+Y)} = e^{tX}~ e^{tY} ~e^{-\frac{t^2}{2} [X,Y]} ~
e^{\frac{t^3}{6}(2[Y,[X,Y]]+ [X,[X,Y]] )} ~
e^{\frac{-t^4}{24}([[[X,Y],X],X] + 3[[[X,Y],X],Y] + 3[[[X,Y],Y],Y]) } \cdots</math>
where the exponents of higher order in {{math|''t''}} are likewise nested commutators, i.e., homogeneous Lie polynomials.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Casas | first1 = F. | last2 = Murua | first2 = A. | last3 = Nadinic | first3 = M. | doi = 10.1016/j.cpc.2012.06.006 | title = Efficient computation of the Zassenhaus formula | journal = Computer Physics Communications | volume = 183 | issue = 11 | pages = 2386–2391 | year = 2012 |arxiv = 1204.0389 |bibcode = 2012CoPhC.183.2386C | s2cid = 2704520 }}</ref>
These exponents, {{math|''C<sub>n</sub>''}} in {{math|1=exp(−''tX'') exp(''t''(''X+Y'')) = Π<sub>''n''</sub> exp(''t<sup>n</sup> C<sub>n</sub>'')}}, follow recursively by application of the above BCH expansion.

As a corollary of this, the [[Lie product formula|Suzuki–Trotter decomposition]] follows.

== Campbell identity ==
The following identity (Campbell 1897) leads to a special case of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula.
Let {{math|''G''}} be a matrix Lie group and {{math|'''g'''}} its corresponding Lie algebra. Let {{math|ad<sub>''X''</sub>}} be the linear operator on {{math|'''g'''}} defined by {{math|1=ad<sub>''X ''</sub> ''Y'' = [''X'',''Y''] = ''XY'' − ''YX''}}  for some fixed {{math| ''X'' ∈ '''g'''}}. (The [[Adjoint representation of a Lie algebra|adjoint endomorphism]] encountered above.) Denote with {{math|Ad<sub>''A''</sub>}} for fixed {{math|''A'' ∈ ''G''}} the linear transformation of {{math|'''g'''}} given by {{math|1=Ad<sub>''A''</sub>''Y'' = ''AYA''<sup>−1</sup>}}.

A standard combinatorial lemma which is utilized<ref name="miller" /> in producing the above explicit expansions is given by<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Proposition 3.35</ref>

{{Math theorem|name=Lemma|note=Campbell 1897|math_statement= 
<math display="block"> \operatorname{Ad}_{e^X} = e^{\operatorname{ad}_X}, </math>
so, explicitly,
<math display="block"> \operatorname{Ad}_{e^X}Y = e^{X}Y e^{-X} = e^{\operatorname{ad} _X} Y =Y+\left[X,Y\right]+\frac{1}{2!}[X,[X,Y]]+\frac{1}{3!}[X,[X,[X,Y]]]+\cdots.</math>
}}

This is a particularly useful formula which is commonly used to conduct [[Unitary transformation (quantum mechanics)|unitary transforms in quantum mechanics]]. By defining the iterated commutator,
<math display="block">[X,Y]_n \equiv \underbrace{[X,\dotsb[X,[X}_{n \text { times }}, Y]] \dotsb],\quad [X,Y]_0 \equiv Y,</math>
we can write this formula more compactly as,
<math display="block">e^X Y e^{-X} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{[X,Y]_n}{n!}.</math>

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=
Evaluate the derivative with respect to {{math|''s''}} of {{math|''f''{{hair space}}(''s'')''Y'' ≡ ''e''<sup>''sX''</sup> ''Y'' ''e''<sup>−''sX''</sup>}}, solution of the resulting differential equation and evaluation at {{math|1=''s'' = 1}},
<math display="block">\frac{d}{ds}f(s)Y = \frac{d}{ds} \left (e^{sX}Ye^{-sX} \right ) = X e^{sX} Y e^{-sX} - e^{sX}Y e^{-sX}X = \operatorname{ad}_X (e^{sX}Ye^{-sX})</math>
or<ref>{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002}} p. 15</ref>
<math display="block"> f'(s) = \operatorname{ad}_Xf(s), \qquad f(0) = 1 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad f(s) = e^{s \operatorname{ad}_X}.</math>
}}

===An application of the identity===
For {{math|[''X'',''Y'']}} central, i.e., commuting with both {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}},
<math display="block">e^{sX} Y e^{-sX} = Y + s [ X, Y ] ~. </math>
Consequently, for {{math|''g''(''s'') ≡ ''e''<sup>''sX''</sup> ''e''<sup>''sY''</sup>}}, it follows that
<math display="block">\frac{dg}{ds} = \Bigl( X+ e^{sX} Y e^{-sX}\Bigr) g(s) = (X + Y + s [ X, Y ]) ~g(s) ~, </math>
whose solution is
<math display="block">g(s)= e^{s(X+Y) +\frac{s^2}{2} [ X, Y ] } ~. </math>
Taking <math>s=1</math> gives one of the special cases of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula described above:
<math display="block">e^X e^Y= e^{X+Y +\frac{1}{2} [ X, Y] } ~. </math>

More generally, for non-central {{math|[''X'',''Y'']}}, we have
<math>e^Xe^Ye^{-X}=e^{e^XYe^{-X}}=e^{e^{\text{ad}_X}Y},</math>
which can be written as the following braiding identity:
<math display="block">e^{X} e^{Y} = e^{(Y+\left[X,Y\right]+\frac{1}{2!}[X,[X,Y]]+\frac{1}{3!}[X,[X,[X,Y]]]+\cdots)} ~e^X.</math>

==Infinitesimal case==
{{main| Derivative of the exponential map}}
A particularly useful variant of the above is the infinitesimal form. This is commonly written as
<math display="block">e^{-X} de^X= dX-\frac{1}{2!}\left[X,dX\right]+\frac{1}{3!}[X,[X,dX]]-\frac{1}{4!}[X,[X,[X,dX]]]+\cdots</math>
This variation is commonly used to write coordinates and [[vielbein]]s as pullbacks of the metric on a Lie group. 

For example, writing <math>X=X^ie_i</math> for some functions <math>X^i</math> and a basis <math>e_i</math> for the Lie algebra, one readily computes that
<math display="block">e^{-X}d e^X= 
   dX^i e_i-\frac{1}{2!} X^i dX^j {f_{ij}}^k e_k +
   \frac{1}{3!} X^iX^j dX^k {f_{jk}}^l {f_{il}}^m e_m - \cdots ,</math>
for <math>[e_i,e_j] = {f_{ij}}^k e_k</math> the [[structure constant]]s of the Lie algebra.  

The series can be written more compactly (cf. main article) as 
<math display="block">e^{-X}d e^X = e_i{W^i}_j dX^j,</math>
with the infinite series 
<math display="block">W = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n M^n}{(n+1)!} = (I-e^{-M}) M^{-1}.</math>
Here, {{mvar|M}} is a matrix whose matrix elements are <math>{M_j}^k = X^i {f_{ij}}^k</math>. 

The usefulness of this expression comes from the fact that the matrix {{mvar|M}}  is a vielbein. Thus, given some map <math>N \to G</math> from some manifold {{mvar|N}} to some manifold {{mvar|G}}, the [[metric tensor]] on the manifold {{mvar|N}} can be written as the pullback of the metric tensor <math>B_{mn}</math> on the Lie group {{mvar|G}},    
<math display="block">g_{ij} = {W_i}^m {W_j}^n B_{mn}.</math>
The metric tensor <math>B_{mn}</math> on the Lie group is the Cartan metric, the [[Killing form]]. For {{mvar|N}} a (pseudo-)[[Riemannian manifold]], the metric is a (pseudo-)[[Riemannian metric]].

== Application in quantum mechanics ==
A special case of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula is useful in [[quantum mechanics]] and especially [[quantum optics]], where {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}} are [[Hilbert space]] operators, generating the [[Heisenberg group|Heisenberg Lie algebra]]. Specifically, the position and momentum operators in quantum mechanics, usually denoted <math>X</math> and <math>P</math>, satisfy the [[canonical commutation relation]]:
<math display="block">[X,P] = i\hbar I</math>
where <math>I</math> is the identity operator. It follows that <math>X</math> and <math>P</math> commute with their commutator. Thus, if we ''formally'' applied a special case of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula (even though <math>X</math> and <math>P</math> are unbounded operators and not matrices), we would conclude that
<math display="block">e^{iaX} e^{ibP} = e^{i \left(aX + bP - \frac{ab\hbar}{2}\right)}.</math>
This "exponentiated commutation relation" does indeed hold, and forms the basis of the [[Stone–von Neumann theorem]]. 
Further,   <math >e^{i(aX+bP)} = e^{iaX/2}e^{ibP}e^{i aX/2} .</math>


A related application is the [[annihilation and creation operators]], {{mvar|''â''}} and {{math|''â''<sup>†</sup>}}. Their commutator {{math|1=[''â''<sup>†</sup>,''â''] = −''I''}} is [[Center (group theory)|''central'']], that is, it commutes with both {{mvar|''â''}} and {{math|''â''<sup>†</sup>}}. As indicated above, the expansion then collapses to the semi-trivial degenerate form:
<math display="block"> e^{v\hat{a}^\dagger - v^*\hat{a}} = e^{v\hat{a}^\dagger} e^{-v^*\hat{a}} e^{-|v|^{2}/2} ,</math>
where {{mvar|v}} is just a [[complex number]].

This example illustrates the resolution of the [[displacement operator]], {{math|exp(''vâ''<sup>†</sup>−''v<sup>*</sup>â'')}}, into exponentials of annihilation and creation operators and scalars.<ref>[[Leonard Mandel|L. Mandel]], [[Emil Wolf|E. Wolf]] ''Optical Coherence and Quantum Optics'' (Cambridge 1995).</ref>

This degenerate Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula then displays the product of two displacement operators as another displacement operator (up to a [[phase factor]]), with the resultant displacement equal to the sum of the two displacements,
<math display="block"> e^{v\hat{a}^\dagger - v^*\hat{a}} e^{u\hat{a}^\dagger - u^*\hat{a}} = e^{(v+u)\hat{a}^\dagger -(v^*+u^*)\hat{a}} e^{(vu^*-uv^*)/2},</math>
since the [[Heisenberg group]] they provide a representation of is [[Nilpotent group|nilpotent]]. The degenerate Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula is frequently used in [[quantum field theory]] as well.<ref>{{harvnb|Greiner|Reinhardt|1996}} See pp 27-29 for a detailed proof of the above lemma.</ref>
